# Wattlyst

> Wattlyst (https://wattlyst.com/) makes free electricity calculators for homes: watts and amps conversions, battery and UPS backup, generator sizing, solar systems, home load and Pakistan electricity bills. Electricity math, done right. Every result shows its formula and assumptions; all calculators run in the browser.

## Sections

- [Appliance Wattage List: Watts and Units per Hour](https://wattlyst.com/appliances/): Running watts, starting watts and units per hour for 60+ home appliances: ACs, fans, fridges, motors, irons, geysers and more. Answer: This appliance wattage list gives the typical running watts, starting (surge) watts and units per hour of common home appliances in Pakistan and the US, from fans and air conditioners to pumps, irons and geysers. Units per hour equal watts divided by one thousand, so a 932 W water pump uses about one unit an hour.
- [Electrical Unit Converters](https://wattlyst.com/converters/): Free electrical converters for watts, amps, volts, kW, kVA, VA and amp hours. Each tool shows the formula with your numbers for DC, single and three phase. Answer: These converters turn one electrical unit into another: watts to amps, amps to watts, kW and kVA, VA to watts and amp hours to watt hours. Pick the supply first, a DC battery, single-phase or three-phase mains, because the same watts draw very different amps on each. Every result shows the formula with your numbers.
- [Battery and UPS Calculators](https://wattlyst.com/battery/): Battery and UPS calculators for homes: backup time, battery bank size and runtime for 12V, 24V and 48V systems, with tubular and lithium battery options. Answer: Battery and UPS calculators answer two questions: how long a battery will run your load, and how big a battery you need for the hours you want. Each one counts only the usable part of the battery, the UPS losses and its own standby draw, for tubular and lithium batteries on twelve, twenty-four and forty-eight volt systems.
- [Generator Calculators](https://wattlyst.com/generator/): Generator calculators for home and appliances: running and starting watts, kVA size, AC and water pump loads, and fuel use, with each step shown. Answer: Generator calculators size a set for what must run during a power cut: the running watts of everything on at once plus the starting surge of the largest motor, turned into kVA with the power factor and rounded up to a size that is sold. They also show what a given kVA can run and what it costs in fuel.
- [Solar Calculators](https://wattlyst.com/solar/): Solar calculators for homes: system size, panels, batteries, inverter, charge controller and net billing, using real sun hours for cities in Pakistan. Answer: Solar calculators size and price a home system from what you use: panels from your daily units and your city's sun, an inverter from the load, a battery from the backup you want, and the bill saving under net billing. Start from your units or your appliance list; every result shows the formula and the city data behind it.
- [Home Load Calculators](https://wattlyst.com/load/): Load calculators for homes: total watts, single phase load, AC units per hour, monthly units and running cost, to plan before adding new appliances. Answer: Home load calculators add up what your appliances draw and use: running watts, the peak with a motor starting, amps, daily and monthly units and what they cost. Use them before adding an AC, before sizing solar, a UPS or a generator, or to check whether your connection's sanctioned load is enough.
- [Bill Calculators for Every DISCO](https://wattlyst.com/bill/): A bill calculator for each DISCO: LESCO, IESCO, MEPCO, GEPCO, FESCO, PESCO, HESCO, SEPCO, QESCO, TESCO and K-Electric, plus FPA and overbilling checks. Answer: Every DISCO in Pakistan, from LESCO and IESCO to K-Electric, bills homes on the same NEPRA domestic tariff, and NEPRA sets one monthly FPA for all of them, so each company's calculator here gives the same bill for the same units. Pick your company below, or use the checks for overbilling, sanctioned load and what an AC adds.
- [Wiring Calculators](https://wattlyst.com/wiring/): Wiring calculators for wire size, MCB breaker size, solar DC cable and voltage drop. Always confirm final wiring with a licensed electrician. Answer: Wiring calculators pick the copper cable and the MCB for a circuit from its load, its length and the kind of load, and check the voltage drop over the run, for mains and for solar DC. They use IEC current ratings for PVC copper cable; have a licensed electrician confirm the final wiring before any work.
- [Electricity Guides](https://wattlyst.com/guides/): Plain-English electricity guides: net billing in Pakistan, peak hours, FPA charges, lithium vs tubular batteries and inverter vs UPS explained. Answer: These guides explain the rules and choices behind the calculators in plain English: net billing and the buyback rate, peak and off-peak hours, the FPA line on your bill, lithium versus tubular batteries, and whether a home needs a UPS or an inverter. Each guide links to the calculator that works out your own numbers.
- [Troubleshooting Tools](https://wattlyst.com/troubleshoot/): Troubleshooting tools for home power systems: look up solar inverter error codes and plan battery series and parallel wiring safely, step by step. Answer: Troubleshooting tools help when the inverter or battery bank is already in the house: look up what an inverter's error code means and whether to call the installer, or plan how to wire batteries in series and parallel for the voltage and amp hours you need, with a diagram. Switch off and isolate before touching any terminal.
- [Pakistan Electricity Data](https://wattlyst.com/data/): Original Pakistan electricity data: a monthly bill index for every DISCO and a solar price tracker, each with a chart, the method and a CSV download. Answer: Wattlyst publishes two original datasets for Pakistan, each refreshed monthly with a chart, its method and a free CSV under CC BY: the Bill Index, the bill at every step of units for every DISCO, and the Solar Price Tracker, dated prices of panels, systems, inverters and batteries from dealer and installer lists.

## Start here

- [Home Power Planner: Free Electricity Calculators](https://wattlyst.com/): Free electricity calculators for Pakistan. The Home Power Planner sizes solar, UPS battery and generator from one appliance list, with bill savings. Answer: The Home Power Planner sizes a home running 2,085 W from one appliance list: an inverter of 3 kW, about 2.5 kWh of battery for 4 hours and 3.51 kW of solar. The best fit is Hybrid solar 3.51 kW + 1 lithium pack of 5.12 kWh (51.2 V), saving about Rs 13,624 a month with your power cuts.

## Calculators

- [Watts to Amps Calculator for DC, Single-Phase and Three-Phase](https://wattlyst.com/converters/watts-to-amps-calculator/): Convert watts to amps for DC, single-phase and three-phase circuits. Pick 12V, 230V or any voltage, add power factor and see the formula with your numbers. Answer: 1,500 watts is 8.15 amps on a 230 V single-phase supply at a power factor of 0.8, or 6.52 A for a heater with a power factor of one. Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor); for DC the power factor is one, and for three-phase the volts are multiplied by the square root of three.
- [Amps to Watts Calculator (DC, AC and 3-Phase)](https://wattlyst.com/converters/amps-to-watts-calculator/): Convert amps to watts for DC, single-phase or three-phase supply. Enter current, voltage and power factor; get watts with a step-by-step formula. Answer: 16 amps on a 230 V single-phase supply is 2,944 watts at a power factor of 0.8, and 3,680 W for a heater with a power factor of one. Watts = amps × volts × power factor; DC uses a power factor of one, and three-phase multiplies by the square root of three.
- [12V Watts to Amps Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/converters/12v-watts-to-amps-calculator/): Find how many amps a 12V load draws from your battery. Includes inverter losses, a 12V reference table and examples for fans, lights and routers. Answer: A 100 W load on a 12 V battery draws about 8.33 A. For DC, amps = watts ÷ volts, with no power factor. Double the voltage and the current halves: a 1,000 W inverter load draws 83.3 A at 12 V but 41.7 A at 24 V, which is why bigger inverters use higher battery voltages.
- [230V and 220V Watts to Amps Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/converters/230v-watts-to-amps-calculator/): Convert watts to amps on 230V or 220V mains. Power factor included, with a table for common appliances like ACs, irons and water motors. Answer: A 1,500 W load on a 230 V single-phase supply draws about 8.15 A at a power factor of 0.8. Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor). A pure heating load has a power factor of one, so a 2,000 W heater draws 8.7 A, while an AC or motor of the same watts draws more.
- [3 Phase Amps Calculator (kW and kVA to Amps)](https://wattlyst.com/converters/3-phase-current-calculator/): Calculate three-phase current from kW or kVA at 400V or any line voltage. Uses I = P / (√3 × V × PF) and shows each step with your values. Answer: A 15 kW three-phase load at 400 V and a power factor of 0.8 draws 27.1 A in each line. Three-phase amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (√3 × line-to-line volts × power factor). For a kVA rating leave out the power factor: a 100 kVA supply carries 144.3 A per line at full load.
- [Amps to kW Calculator (and kW to Amps)](https://wattlyst.com/converters/amps-to-kw-calculator/): Convert amps to kilowatts and back for DC, single-phase and three-phase supply. Add power factor, see the formula and a quick reference table. Answer: 32 amps on a 230 V single-phase supply is 5.89 kW at a power factor of 0.8. kW = amps × volts × power factor ÷ 1,000, with √3 added for three-phase, where 32 A per line at 400 V is 17.74 kW. For kW to amps, choose kW to amps above: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor), so 5 kW on single-phase is 27.17 A.
- [Volts to Watts Calculator (Volts × Amps)](https://wattlyst.com/converters/volts-to-watts-calculator/): Turn volts and amps into watts for DC or AC circuits. Includes power factor for AC loads and worked examples for 12V, 24V and 230V. Answer: 230 volts at 5 amps is 1,150 VA, which is 920 watts at a power factor of 0.8 or 1,150 W for a heater. Watts = volts × amps × power factor. Volts alone do not give watts: you need the current too. On DC the power factor is one, so 12 V at 5 A is 60 W.
- [kVA to kW Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/converters/kva-to-kw-calculator/): Convert kVA to kW using power factor. See why a 5 kVA generator or UPS gives about 4 kW at PF 0.8, with a table for common sizes. Answer: A 5 kVA generator or UPS delivers about 4 kW of real power at a power factor of 0.8. kW = kVA × power factor. The kVA figure is the apparent power the machine can carry; the kW is the useful power your appliances get, so a 10 kVA set gives 8 kW and a 3.5 kVA set about 2.8 kW.
- [VA to Watts Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/converters/va-to-watts-calculator/): Convert a UPS or inverter VA rating to real watts using power factor. Find how many watts a 1000VA or 1500VA UPS can actually run. Answer: A 1,000 VA UPS can run about 600 W of real load at a power factor of 0.6, the usual figure for a line-interactive home or PC UPS. Watts = VA × power factor. An online UPS or inverter rated at 0.8 gives 800 W from the same 1,000 VA, so always read the power factor on the label.
- [Amp Hours to Watt Hours (Ah to Wh) Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/converters/ah-to-wh-calculator/): Convert battery amp-hours to watt-hours or kWh, and back. Pick 12V, 24V, 48V or 51.2V lithium; the page shows how depth of discharge cuts usable energy. Answer: A 200 Ah battery at 12 V stores 2,400 Wh, which is 2.4 kWh or 2.4 units. Watt hours = amp hours × volts. A 100 Ah battery at the same voltage holds 1.2 kWh, and a 100 Ah battery on a 48 V bank holds 4.8 kWh. Only part of this is usable; see depth of discharge below.
- [Battery Backup Time Calculator for Home](https://wattlyst.com/battery/battery-backup-time-calculator/): How long will your home UPS battery last? Enter load, battery Ah and type (tubular or lithium) to get backup time with inverter losses included. Answer: A 200 Ah, 12 V tubular battery runs a 300 W load for about 3 hours through a UPS while using only the recommended 50% of its capacity. Backup time equals battery Ah × volts × usable depth of discharge ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw).
- [12V Battery Runtime Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/battery/12v-battery-runtime-calculator/): Find how long a 12V battery runs your load. Works for 100Ah, 150Ah and 200Ah, lead-acid or lithium, with DC and inverter loads. Answer: A 100 Ah, 12 V lead-acid battery runs a 100 W load through an inverter for about 4 h 3 min, using only the 50% of its capacity that is safe to use. Runtime in hours equals Ah × volts × usable depth of discharge ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw); for a DC load set the efficiency to one.
- [200Ah Battery Backup Time Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/battery/200ah-battery-backup-time-calculator/): See how many hours a 200Ah battery runs fans, lights, a fridge or a PC. Tubular and lithium, 12V or 24V, with a ready backup time table. Answer: A 200 Ah, 12 V tubular battery gives about 3 h 8 min of backup for a 300 W load (a fan, lights and a TV) through a home UPS, using the safe 50% of its capacity. Backup hours = Ah × volts × usable depth of discharge ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw); the chart below shows common loads.
- [Battery Capacity Calculator for Appliances](https://wattlyst.com/battery/battery-bank-size-calculator/): Pick your appliances and backup hours to get the battery Ah and how many batteries you need for a 1kW, 3kW or 5kW inverter. Tubular and lithium. Answer: To run 500 W of appliances for 4 hours on a 24 V inverter you need a 207 Ah tubular battery bank: 4 batteries of 200 Ah, 2 in series. Battery Ah = (watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw) × hours ÷ (bank volts × usable depth of discharge); batteries = bank Ah ÷ one battery's Ah, times the batteries in series.
- [UPS Backup Time Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/battery/ups-backup-time-calculator/): Estimate UPS runtime for a PC, router or CCTV from VA rating, battery Ah and load. Includes power factor and real inverter efficiency. Answer: A 1,000 VA UPS with a 150 Ah, 12 V tubular battery runs a 300 W desktop PC for about 2 h 21 min. The UPS can deliver at most 600 W (1,000 VA × 0.6 power factor), so this load uses 50% of it. Backup hours = Ah × volts × usable depth ÷ (load watts ÷ inverter efficiency + the inverter's idle draw).
- [Generator Size Calculator for Home](https://wattlyst.com/generator/generator-size-calculator/): Find the right generator size in kVA and watts for your home. Add AC, fridge, motor and lights; starting surge and a safety margin included. Answer: A home with four fans, ten LED bulbs, an inverter fridge, a TV, a 1.5 ton inverter AC and a 1 hp water motor needs a 6.5 kVA generator: 3,017 W running, 4,881 W when the pump starts. kVA = the larger of running watts × 1.25 or peak watts, ÷ 0.8 power factor ÷ 1,000.
- [Generator Watts Calculator for Appliances](https://wattlyst.com/generator/generator-wattage-calculator/): Add up running and starting watts of your appliances to size a generator, using our list of common home appliances with typical watts. Answer: Three fans, six LED bulbs, a TV, a non-inverter fridge and a router run at 597 W and peak at 1,597 W when the fridge starts, so the generator must deliver 1,597 W, a 2.5 kVA set. Generator watts = the larger of total running watts × 1.25 or running watts plus the biggest starting surge.
- [Generator Starting Watts Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/generator/generator-starting-watts-calculator/): Work out the peak starting watts your generator must handle for ACs, fridges and pumps, and why only the biggest motor's surge counts. Answer: With four fans, ten bulbs, a non-inverter fridge, a 1 hp water motor and a twin-tub washer on, the generator must supply 3,836 W when the pump starts, against 1,972 W running, so 5 kVA. Starting watts = total running watts + the largest single starting jump (starting minus running watts of the biggest motor), not the sum of every surge.
- [Running Watts vs Starting Watts Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/generator/running-vs-starting-watts/): See running and starting watts side by side for each appliance, and how they decide your generator or inverter size. Table and calculator. Answer: Running watts are the steady power an appliance draws while it works; starting watts are the short burst a motor or compressor needs for a second or two to get going. A non-inverter fridge runs at 200 W but starts at 1,200 W, so a generator must deliver 1,200 W. Size on the larger of running watts × 1.25 or starting watts.
- [Generator Size for Well Pump](https://wattlyst.com/generator/generator-for-well-pump/): Find the generator size for a 0.5 to 5 HP well or water pump. Converts HP to watts, adds motor starting surge and gives kVA at PF 0.8. Answer: A 1 hp well pump draws about 932 W while running and about 2,796 W for a second or two while it starts. That surge needs about 3.5 kVA, so the generator to buy is the next standard size, 3.5 kVA. Generator kVA = the larger of running watts × margin or starting watts, ÷ power factor ÷ 1,000.
- [Generator Size for 1.5 Ton AC](https://wattlyst.com/generator/generator-for-1-5-ton-ac/): What kVA generator runs a 1.5 ton inverter or non-inverter AC? Running and starting watts, kVA at PF 0.8, and home load examples. Answer: A 1.5 ton inverter AC with 500 W of fans and lights needs a 3.5 kVA generator: 1,950 W running, 2,400 W while the compressor starts, 3.05 kVA calculated. A 1.5 ton non-inverter AC with the same load needs 7.5 kVA because its compressor starts at 5,400 W. Generator kVA = max(running watts × margin, starting watts) ÷ power factor ÷ 1,000.
- [What Can a 5 kVA Generator Run?](https://wattlyst.com/generator/what-can-a-kva-generator-run/): See which appliances a 3, 5 or 7 kVA generator can run at once, with real watts at PF 0.8 and motor starting surge. Try your own list. Answer: A 5 kVA generator gives 4,000 W at 0.8 power factor: about 3,200 W of continuous running load and 4,000 W for the moment a motor starts. That runs 2 inverter ACs of 1.5 ton on their own, or one 1.5 ton inverter AC with fans, lights, a fridge and a TV (2,085 W). Usable watts = kVA × 1,000 × power factor.
- [Generator Fuel Consumption Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/generator/generator-fuel-consumption-calculator/): Estimate petrol or diesel use per hour and the running cost in PKR for your generator size and load, with the cost per unit compared to the grid. Answer: A 5 kVA petrol generator carrying 2,000 W burns about 1.36 litres an hour, Rs 520 an hour at Rs 382.02 a litre; a diesel set of the same size uses about 0.7 litres. Fuel per hour = an idle amount per rated kW + an amount per kW of load; cost per hour = litres × fuel price.
- [Solar Battery Size Calculator for Home](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-battery-size-calculator/): Size the battery bank for your solar system from night-time load, backup days and battery type. Lithium and tubular, 12V to 48V. Answer: A home that uses 5 units from the battery each night needs a solar battery bank of about 129 Ah at 48 V (6.2 kWh) with lithium batteries, for 1 day of autonomy. Battery Ah = night units × days ÷ (bank volts × usable depth of discharge × inverter efficiency); a tubular bank must be almost twice as large.
- [Solar Panel Wattage Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-panel-wattage-calculator/): Find the total solar panel watts you need from daily kWh and your city's sun hours. Losses included; shows the number of 585W panels. Answer: For a bill of 300 units a month in Lahore you need about 2.47 kW of solar panel wattage, which is 5 panels of 585 W (2.93 kW installed) on about 12.9 m² of roof. Panel watts = daily units ÷ the units one kW of panels makes a day in your city, rounded up to whole panels.
- [Off-Grid Solar System Size Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/solar/off-grid-solar-calculator/): Plan a full off-grid solar system: panels, battery bank, inverter and charge controller from your appliance list and backup days. Answer: A small off-grid house with three fans, eight LED bulbs, an inverter fridge, a TV, a pump and a router needs 1.76 kW of panels (3 panels), a 118 Ah lithium bank at 48 V for 4 hours of the full load after sunset, and a 1.43 kW inverter. Panels = (day units + night units ÷ charging and inverter efficiency) ÷ sun yield; battery = night units ÷ (volts × usable share × efficiency).
- [Inverter Size Calculator for Home Appliances](https://wattlyst.com/solar/inverter-size-calculator/): Find the inverter or UPS size in watts and kVA for your appliances, including AC and motor starting surge. Can a UPS run a 1 ton AC? Answer: Three fans, eight LED bulbs, a TV, an inverter fridge and a 1 ton inverter AC draw 1,431 W together, so the inverter needs a continuous rating of at least 1,789 W, about 2.24 kVA, with a surge rating of 1,921 W for the AC's step up to full speed, the largest in the list. Inverter watts = running load × margin; kVA = watts ÷ power factor ÷ 1,000.
- [How Many Solar Panels Do I Need to Run an AC?](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-panels-to-run-ac/): Find the solar panels, inverter and battery to run a 1 or 1.5 ton inverter AC in Pakistan. Uses your city's sun hours and real AC watts. Answer: A 1.5 ton inverter AC running 8 hours a day in Lahore needs 4 solar panels of 585 W (2.34 kW installed) and a 1.82 kW inverter, with no battery for daytime use. It uses about 8 units a day, and each kW of panels in Lahore makes about 4 units a day.
- [Solar Panel Calculator for 12V Battery](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-panel-for-12v-battery/): What size solar panel charges a 100Ah or 200Ah 12V battery? Includes charge controller type, sun hours and charging losses. Answer: A 100 Ah 12 V lead-acid battery needs at least a 181 W solar panel to put back half its charge in 5 peak sun hours, so buy a 200 W panel with a 30 A MPPT charge controller. That panel refills the battery in about 4.5 hours of peak sun. Panel watts = Ah × V × depth of discharge ÷ charging efficiency ÷ (sun hours × performance ratio).
- [Solar System Size for Daily kWh Usage](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-system-size-calculator/): Turn your daily kWh usage or monthly units into solar system size in kW, panel count and roof space, using real sun data for your city. Answer: A home that uses 15.8 units a day in Lahore needs a solar system of about 3.95 kW, installed as 7 panels of 585 W (4.1 kW) on about 18.1 m² of roof, making about 498 units a month. Solar system kW = daily kWh ÷ the units one kW makes a day in your city.
- [Solar System for 5 Marla House](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-system-for-5-marla-house/): How many kW solar does a 5 marla house need? Typical load, panels, inverter, battery and cost, plus a calculator for your own bill. Answer: A typical 5 marla house with fans, LED lights, an inverter fridge, a TV, one 1.5 ton inverter AC, a water pump and an iron needs a solar system of about 4.1 kW (7 panels of 585 W) with an on-grid inverter of 3.6 kW. The panels are sized from the daily units ÷ the city's sun yield; the grid covers the moments when everything runs at once.
- [Solar Panel Price in Pakistan Today: Per Watt and Per Panel](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-panel-price-pakistan/): Today's solar panel prices in Pakistan per watt and per panel for 550W to 600W+ brands, with the date checked and a cost calculator. Answer: A 585 W solar panel costs about Rs 23,400 to Rs 26,600 in Pakistan today, at the typical retail rate of Rs 40 to Rs 45.5 per watt for tier-one N-type panels (checked 2026-10-14). Panel price = panel watts × rupees per watt, so 10 panels cost Rs 234,000 to Rs 266,000, panels only.
- [Net Billing Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/solar/net-billing-calculator/): Compare your bill under old net metering and the 2026 net billing rules. Enter units imported and exported; see the bill and the export credit in PKR. Answer: A home that imports 400 units and exports 300 units pays about Rs 12,145 in energy charges under net billing, against Rs 2,244 under old net metering, so net billing costs Rs 9,901 more that month. Net bill = imported units × slab rate − exported units × buyback rate of Rs 8.13.
- [10 Marla Solar System: Size, Panels and Inverter](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-system-for-10-marla-house/): Typical 10 marla load, the right solar system size in kW, panels, inverter and battery, plus cost and payback. Use the calculator for your bill. Answer: A typical 10 marla house with six fans, lights, an inverter fridge, a deep freezer, two TVs, three inverter ACs, a water pump, an iron and a washing machine needs a solar system of about 8.78 kW (15 panels) with an on-grid inverter of 8 kW. Panels = daily units ÷ sun yield; the grid covers the moments when everything runs at once.
- [1 Kanal Solar System: Size for a House with 3 to 4 ACs](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-system-for-1-kanal-house/): How much solar does a 1 kanal house need with 3 to 4 ACs? kW, panels, hybrid inverter, battery options and cost estimate. Answer: A typical 1 kanal house with four inverter ACs, eight fans, lights, an inverter fridge, a deep freezer, two large TVs, a 1.5 hp water pump and kitchen appliances needs a solar system of about 13.46 kW (23 panels) with a three-phase on-grid inverter of 12 kW. Panels = daily units ÷ sun yield; the grid covers the moments when everything runs at once.
- [Solar System Price in Pakistan: 3kW, 5kW and 10kW Systems](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-system-price-pakistan/): Estimated price of a 3kW, 5kW or 10kW on-grid or hybrid solar system in Pakistan, in rupees and lakh, with the panel share, the date checked and a payback. Answer: A 10 kW on-grid solar system in Pakistan costs about Rs 950,000 to Rs 1,200,000 (Rs 9.5 lakh to Rs 12 lakh) installed (Rs 95 to Rs 120 per watt) in the installer price lists under Sources; a hybrid system costs more. If it removes Rs 25,000 a month from the bill, the simple payback is 3.2 to 4 years.
- [Tubewell Solar System Calculator: HP to kW](https://wattlyst.com/solar/tubewell-solar-calculator/): Size a solar system for a 1 to 20 HP tubewell or water pump: panel kW, VFD inverter and daily water hours. For farmers in Pakistan. Answer: A 10 hp tubewell pumping 6 hours a day near Multan needs a solar array of about 16.38 kW (28 panels of 585 W) and a solar pump drive of 15 kW, with no battery. Pump watts = hp × 745.7 ÷ motor efficiency; the array is the larger of daily units ÷ sun yield and pump watts ÷ performance ratio.
- [Solar Charge Controller Size Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/solar/charge-controller-size-calculator/): Find the amp rating of your PWM or MPPT solar charge controller from panel watts, short-circuit amps and battery voltage, with a safety margin. Answer: 1,000 W of solar panels on a 24 V battery needs an MPPT solar charge controller of at least 52.1 A, so buy the next size sold, a 60 A controller. MPPT amps = total panel watts ÷ battery volts × a safety margin of 1.25; a PWM controller is sized from the panel short-circuit current × panels in parallel × the same margin.
- [Home Electrical Load Calculator](https://wattlyst.com/load/home-electrical-load-calculator/): Add your home appliances to get total watts, peak load, amps and daily units. Pakistani and US appliance lists, then size your UPS or solar. Answer: A typical home with 18 appliances running together (fans, lights, a fridge, a TV, a 1.5 ton inverter AC and a water pump) draws about 3,017 W, or 15.4 A at 230 V, and uses about 458 units a month. Add your own appliances below to get your total watts, peak load, amps and monthly units.

- [Wire Size for 1.5 Ton AC](https://wattlyst.com/wiring/wire-size-for-1-5-ton-ac/): Which wire and breaker for a 1.5 ton inverter or non-inverter AC? mm² and 3/29, 7/29 sizes, run length and safety margin, explained. It is sized at the AC's maximum input of 1,900 W: 9.2 A design current with a 1.25 × margin, and the voltage drop is only 1.1%.

Answer: A 2,000 W single-phase load over a 20 m run in conduit needs a 2.5 mm² copper cable (7/29 in Pakistani sizes), rated 19 A, on a 16 A MCB, with a 1.7% voltage drop. The cable must carry the design current of 10.9 A times a 1.25 safety margin and keep the drop under 5%.

Wire and breaker matched safely. Answer: A 2,000 W socket circuit on 230 V draws 10.9 A, so the MCB is the next standard size up: 16 A, type C, on at least 2.5 mm² (7/29) copper cable. MCB rating = next standard size above watts ÷ (volts × power factor); motor-type loads add a 1.25 × margin, and the curve follows the load type.
- [DC Cable Size for Solar Panels](https://wattlyst.com/wiring/solar-cable-size-calculator/): Size the DC cable from solar panels to inverter and battery for 3kW to 10kW systems. Keeps voltage drop under 3% with a safety margin. Answer: A 4 mm² DC cable from solar panels carrying 14 A at 420 V over a 25 m run loses 3.9 V, a 0.94% voltage drop, within the 3% limit for solar DC, so 4 mm² is the right size for this string. Drop = two × length × current × copper resistivity ÷ cable area; move up to 6 mm² when the drop passes the limit.
- [Voltage Drop Calculator for Any Cable, AC or DC](https://wattlyst.com/wiring/voltage-drop-calculator/): Calculate voltage drop for any wire size, length and load, single or three phase, DC or AC. See if your cable stays under 3% or 5%. Answer: A 16.3 A load on 2.5 mm² copper cable over 30 m at 230 V loses 8.8 V, a voltage drop of 3.83%, under the 5% limit. Voltage drop = two × length × current × resistivity ÷ cable area for single-phase and DC; three-phase uses √3 instead of two. The cable must also be rated for the current, which the calculator checks for copper.

Series adds the volts (bank V = batteries in series × battery V), parallel adds the amp hours (bank Ah = strings × battery Ah), and kWh = bank V × bank Ah ÷ 1000.
- [Solar Panel Cleaning Loss Calculator: Dust and When to Clean](https://wattlyst.com/solar/solar-panel-cleaning-loss-calculator/): Estimate how many units and rupees dust is costing your solar system each day, and after how many days a cleaning pays for itself. Answer: A 24 V 200 Ah tubular battery bank carries a 2,000 Wh daily load for about 1.5 cloudy days when the panels still make 600 Wh a day. Days of autonomy = (Ah × V × depth of discharge × inverter efficiency) ÷ (daily load in Wh − cloudy-day solar in Wh). Lithium, at a deeper discharge, lasts longer from the same Ah.

## Guides

- [Net Billing in Pakistan: Rules, Buyback Rate and Net Metering Compared](https://wattlyst.com/guides/net-billing-pakistan/): What changed from net metering to net billing in Pakistan, the export rate, who keeps old contracts and what it means for solar payback. Answer: Net billing in Pakistan charges every imported unit at your normal slab rate and credits each exported unit at a flat buyback rate, Rs 8.13 for CY 2026 (NEPRA's national average energy purchase price). Net bill = imports × slab rate − exports × buyback rate: importing 400 and exporting 300 units costs Rs 12,145, against Rs 2,244 under old net metering.
- [Peak Hours LESCO 2026: Latest NEPRA Schedule for Every DISCO (2023 Determination)](https://wattlyst.com/guides/peak-hours-pakistan/): Peak and off-peak hours by season for LESCO, IESCO and other DISCOs from NEPRA's latest schedule (2023, not re-confirmed for 2026) and what shifting saves. Answer: Peak hours for LESCO and the other ex-WAPDA DISCOs are 6 pm to 10 pm in September to November, 5 pm to 9 pm in December to February, 6 pm to 10 pm in March to May and 7 pm to 11 pm in June to August, per NEPRA's 2023 IESCO schedule, not yet re-confirmed for 2026. On a time-of-use meter (5 kW and above) 800 units cost about Rs 42,251.
- [FPA in Electricity Bill: What It Means and How to Calculate It](https://wattlyst.com/guides/fpa-in-electricity-bill/): What fuel price adjustment (FPA) means on your bill, the latest NEPRA-verified rate with the decision link, and how to calculate it yourself. Answer: FPA (fuel price adjustment) is NEPRA's monthly per-unit charge or credit for the fuel cost gap. October 2026 bills carry Rs 1.11 per unit for August 2026, reported in the news. FPA line = rate × the units of the FPA month (not this month's): at the pre-filled July 2026 rate (latest NEPRA-verified), 300 units add Rs 617, plus GST.
- [Lithium vs Tubular Battery: Backup, Life and Cost](https://wattlyst.com/guides/lithium-vs-tubular-battery/): Lithium vs tubular battery compared on usable backup, cycle life, charging, price per usable kWh and which suits loadshedding. Answer: A lithium (LiFePO4) battery gives nearly twice the usable backup of a tubular battery of the same rated Ah and volts, because it can be used to about 90% of its capacity against about 50% for tubular, charges faster with less loss, and lasts several times as many cycles. The tubular battery costs far less to buy, so the fair comparison is price per usable unit over its life.
- [Inverter vs UPS: Which One for Your Home?](https://wattlyst.com/guides/inverter-vs-ups/): The real difference between a UPS, an inverter and a hybrid solar inverter, with switching time, efficiency and which loads each can run. Answer: A UPS switches to battery within a few milliseconds so computers never notice the cut; an inverter switches a little slower but runs bigger loads, and a hybrid solar inverter also charges from solar panels. In Pakistan the words overlap: most home UPS units are really inverters with a built-in charger. Choose by what you need to run and for how long.

## Data (CC BY 4.0, CSV download on each page)

- [Pakistan Electricity Bill Index](https://wattlyst.com/data/pakistan-electricity-bill-index/): Monthly bill for every 50 units from 50 to 1,000 in LESCO, IESCO, K-Electric and every DISCO, protected and unprotected, with method and a free CSV. Answer: In October 2026 bills, an unprotected home using 300 units pays about Rs 14,264, down Rs 335 (2.3%) from September 2026, mainly because the fuel price adjustment moved from Rs 2.06 to Rs 1.11 per unit. The same uniform tariff applies in LESCO, IESCO, MEPCO, K-Electric and every other DISCO. Bill = energy + fixed charge + surcharges + GST.
- [Pakistan Solar Price Tracker](https://wattlyst.com/data/pakistan-solar-price-tracker/): Monthly tracker of solar system, panel, inverter and battery prices in Pakistan from dealer price lists, each with its source and date, and a CSV. Answer: Solar prices in Pakistan, checked 2026-10-14: Tier-1 panels cost Rs 40 to Rs 45.5 per watt, about Rs 23,400 to Rs 26,600 for a 585 W panel. A 10 kW on-grid system costs Rs 950,000 to Rs 1,200,000 installed and a 10 kW hybrid Rs 1,400,000 to Rs 1,800,000, from dated dealer and installer price lists.
